entities.name: Jean Le Maingre
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean II Le Maingre, known primarily as Boucicaut, was a towering figure of late medieval French chivalry and military command, serving as Marshal of France from 1391 until his capture at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Born into a distinguished noble family in Touraine around 1366, Boucicaut's career spanned the tumultuous Hundred Years' War and the broader European conflicts of the late 14th and early 15th centuries. He is remembered not only for his martial prowess and innovative military strategies but also for embodying the ideals of knighthood, founding the chivalric Order of the White Lady, and crusading against the Ottoman Empire.

Boucicaut's early military experience included campaigns in Prussia and the Balkans, notably participating in the disastrous Crusade of Nicopolis in 1396, where he was captured and later ransomed. His strategic brilliance was evident in his defense of Constantinople against Ottoman siege in 1399-1402, and his subsequent appointment as Governor of Genoa from 1401 to 1409 saw him expand Genoese influence across the Mediterranean, including campaigns against Cyprus and Venice. Returning to France, he became a key commander for King Charles VI, fighting against the English and Burgundians. His final major engagement was at Agincourt in 1415, where, despite his experience, he was among the French commanders captured by Henry V's forces, dying in English captivity six years later.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jean Le Maingre was a leading military figure and exemplar of chivalry in late medieval France, whose career directly impacted the course of the Hundred Years' War and European crusading efforts. His governorship of Genoa and participation in major battles like Nicopolis and Agincourt left a tangible mark on the geopolitical landscape of the early 15th century.
